predictions.explanation:
Assessing the three main components of Sacks’s prediction against what actually happened by the California recall election on **September 14, 2021**:

1. **"The economy is going to be booming again"**  
   *At the national level, this was broadly accurate.*
   - Real U.S. GDP grew about **5.9–6.2% in 2021**, the fastest annual growth since the mid‑1980s, reflecting a strong post‑COVID rebound. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden?utm_source=openai))  
   - The unemployment rate fell from **6.1% in April 2021** to **4.8% by September 2021**, a steep improvement, even though the September jobs report (194,000 jobs added vs. ~500,000 expected) disappointed forecasters. ([bls.gov](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2021/u-3-was-6-1-percent-u-6-was-10-4-percent-in-april-2021.htm?utm_source=openai))  
   Overall, many economists and officials described the 2021 recovery as very strong; calling the economy “booming” is defensible.

2. **"COVID's going to be over" (as an issue by the recall)**  
   *This was clearly false.*
   - The **Delta variant wave** peaked in mid‑September 2021, with around **127,000 new U.S. cases per day**, and hospitals across the country were again in crisis conditions. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_hospital_crisis_in_the_U.S._from_COVID-19?utm_source=openai))  
   - By mid‑September, the U.S. had surpassed **40 million cases** and more than **675,000 deaths**, exceeding estimated U.S. deaths from the 1918 flu; by early October, deaths passed 700,000. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States?utm_source=openai))  
   - In the **California recall exit polls**, roughly **one‑third of voters** said the **ongoing COVID‑19 pandemic** was the most important issue facing the state—the single top concern—indicating COVID was very much *not* “over” as a major political or public concern. ([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/california-recall-cbs-news-exit-poll-shows-voters-most-concerned-about-covid-economy/?utm_source=openai))

3. **"People will probably forget" Newsom’s earlier vaccine/ COVID missteps**  
   *Partly but not fully accurate; voters didn’t forget the pandemic, but earlier anger over vaccine rollout largely faded.*
   - Early 2021 polling (e.g., Berkeley IGS in February) found **strong dissatisfaction** with Newsom’s handling of COVID and especially **vaccine distribution**—only about **22–29%** rated vaccine rollout as good or excellent, and his pandemic handling was widely criticized. ([calmatters.org](https://calmatters.org/commentary/2021/02/california-polls-newsom-approval-recall/?utm_source=openai))  
   - By **September 2021**, however, a PPIC survey cited in CNBC found that **over three‑quarters of Californians** thought the state government was doing an **“excellent or good” job** distributing COVID vaccines, and **roughly 6 in 10** approved of Newsom’s overall pandemic response. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/09/17/california-counties-with-high-covid-vaccination-rates-helped-newsom-win-the-recall-election.html?utm_source=openai))  
   - High‑vaccination counties voted strongly to keep Newsom, and analyses of the recall emphasized that his pro‑vaccine, pro‑mandate stance had become a political *asset*, not a liability; Newsom explicitly framed his victory as a mandate for his COVID and vaccination policies. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/09/17/california-counties-with-high-covid-vaccination-rates-helped-newsom-win-the-recall-election.html?utm_source=openai))  
   So, while voters absolutely had *not* “forgotten” COVID—the issue was front and center in their minds—they had largely **moved past or forgiven** the earlier vaccine‑rollout problems by the time of the recall.

**Overall judgment**  
- The **economic** part of the prediction was broadly right.  
- The **central claim that “COVID’s going to be over” and thus no longer a major issue** was decisively wrong: the Delta surge was peaking, and COVID was the top issue in California’s recall. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States?utm_source=openai))  
- Voters didn’t forget the pandemic; instead, they ended up largely *approving* of Newsom’s later COVID/vaccine policies and kept him in office.

Because the most consequential part of the scenario—COVID being effectively “over” as a major issue by the recall—turned out to be incorrect, the overall prediction is best classified as **wrong**, albeit with some partially correct components about economic recovery and the fading of anger over the initial vaccine rollout.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence on both interest rates and growth-stock valuations lines up broadly with E’s call.

• **10‑year Treasury path.** In April 2021, when the episode was released, the 10‑year Treasury yield averaged about **1.63%**. By January 2022 it had risen to **1.76%**, and then to **1.93% in February** and **2.13% in March**, reaching **2.75% by April 2022**. So during the subsequent normalization period the yield moved *through* and beyond the ~1.8% area E mentioned. ([multpl.com](https://www.multpl.com/10-year-treasury-rate/table/by-month?utm_source=openai))

• **Starting point for growth multiples.** Ed Yardeni noted in late 2021 that the **S&P 500 Growth index forward P/E had been “hovering around 28.0 since mid‑2020”**, i.e., it stayed roughly in that high‑20s range through 2021. That implies that around mid‑April 2021, growth‑stock forward P/Es were close to ~28x. ([archive.yardeni.com](https://archive.yardeni.com/morning-briefing-2021/?utm_source=openai))

• **Subsequent compression of growth multiples.** Yardeni later documented that **from the start of 2022 to April 30, 2022** the **S&P 500 Growth forward P/E fell from 28.3 to 21.0**, a drop of about **26%** ((21.0 ÷ 28.3) − 1 ≈ −25.8%). ([yardeniquicktakes.com](https://www.yardeniquicktakes.com/inflation-is-deflating-valuation-multiples/?utm_source=openai)) By early May 2022 he reported the S&P 500 Growth forward P/E at **~20.8**, confirming that the multiple had indeed fallen a bit more than 25% from its high‑20s level. ([yardeniquicktakes.com](https://www.yardeniquicktakes.com/more-air-coming-out-of-valuation-multiples/?utm_source=openai))

• **Timing vs. yields.** This ~25%+ compression in growth multiples occurred over the same period that the 10‑year yield moved from roughly **1.6% in April 2021** to **around 1.8–2.1% in early 2022** and then further up toward **2.75% by April 2022**. ([multpl.com](https://www.multpl.com/10-year-treasury-rate/table/by-month?utm_source=openai)) While the biggest part of the compression occurred as yields *overshot* 1.8% (into the mid‑2s), the direction and order of magnitude of the move are consistent with E’s thesis that higher rates would drive another ~10–20% valuation reset in growth equities.

Putting this together, growth‑equity forward P/Es did in fact compress on the order of **10–20% (and ultimately a bit more, ~25%)** as the 10‑year yield normalized upward from its April 2021 level toward and beyond ~1.8%. The magnitude and mechanism E described were broadly correct, even though the eventual compression somewhat exceeded his 10–20% range and coincided with yields rising past, not just to, 1.8%. Therefore the prediction is best classified as **right** in substance, with the caveat that the move was larger than he anticipated.

predictions.explanation:
Looking at the roughly three‑month window after mid‑April 2021 (≈April 17–July 17, 2021), there is evidence of *some* further valuation multiple compression, especially when you include fundamentals, not just prices.

1. **Broad U.S. equity market (S&P 500)**  
   * Price: The S&P 500 closed at 4,185 on April 16, 2021 and 4,327 on July 16, 2021, a gain of about 3–4%. ([statmuse.com](https://www.statmuse.com/money/ask/sandp-500-april-2021?utm_source=openai))  
   * Multiples: FactSet’s earnings reports show the S&P 500 forward 12‑month P/E at **22.0** on April 30, 2021 and **21.3** on July 23, 2021. ([insight.factset.com](https://insight.factset.com/sp-500-earnings-season-update-april-30-2021?utm_source=openai))  Over that period, earnings estimates were being revised sharply upward (Q2 2021 earnings growth was described as the strongest since 2009), meaning prices rose less than forward earnings, so the aggregate P/E multiple *did* compress modestly even as the index hit new highs. ([insight.factset.com](https://insight.factset.com/sp-500-earnings-season-update-july-16-2021?utm_source=openai))  
   * Another commentator characterizes the S&P 500’s P/E as being around ~22x “about where the PE has been all year,” but that’s broadly consistent with *slight* compression rather than renewed multiple expansion. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/analysis/sp-500-earnings-update-sp-500s-forward-estimate-increases-are-remarkable-200595238?utm_source=openai))

2. **Growth / high‑multiple segment**  
   * A good proxy for high‑growth, high‑multiple stocks is the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK). ARKK closed at **$124.38** on April 16, 2021 and **$116.53** on July 16, 2021, a decline of about **6%** over the window. ([financecharts.com](https://www.financecharts.com/etfs/ARKK/summary/price?utm_source=openai))  In between, it sold off more sharply in May before partially recovering, which is exactly the sort of “more compression” he was worried about.  
   * Many of ARKK’s underlying holdings were still reporting very rapid revenue growth in 2021, so a flat‑to‑down price over that period implies **lower price‑to‑sales and price‑to‑earnings multiples**—i.e., further multiple compression relative to fundamentals.
   * Sector commentary at the time noted that by early March 2021 SaaS/growth EV/Sales multiples had already fallen by roughly one‑third from their peaks, yet they were still high; this context supports the idea that an ongoing de‑rating of growth names was underway around and after April. ([gauchorico.com](https://gauchorico.com/big-drops/?utm_source=openai))  Russell style data also show value sharply outperforming growth into May 2021, consistent with pressure on growth‑stock valuations. ([lseg.com](https://www.lseg.com/en/media-centre/press-releases/ftse-russell/2021/ftse-russell-begins-33rd-annual-russell-us-indexes-reconstitution?utm_source=openai))

3. **Tech / Nasdaq context**  
   The Nasdaq‑100 rose from 14,000 on April 15, 2021 to 15,000 by July 23, 2021 (≈+7%), while large‑cap tech earnings were also being revised higher. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdaq-100?utm_source=openai))  That pattern—earnings rising faster than prices—again implies at worst flat and more likely *slightly lower* forward multiples for that growth‑heavy index over the period.

Overall, the data show that from mid‑April to mid‑July 2021:

* Broad U.S. equity valuations (e.g., S&P 500 forward P/E) **edged down**, not up, despite higher prices, because earnings estimates rose even faster. ([insight.factset.com](https://insight.factset.com/sp-500-earnings-season-update-april-30-2021?utm_source=openai))  
* High‑multiple growth names, as proxied by ARKK and the documented style rotation from growth to value, experienced **further pressure on prices relative to fundamentals**, i.e., more multiple compression. ([financecharts.com](https://www.financecharts.com/etfs/ARKK/summary/price?utm_source=openai))

The compression was modest and far from a crash, and much of the *big* de‑rating had already occurred in Q1 2021. But on the literal question of whether there was **more** multiple compression in public markets—especially in growth stocks—over the next three months after mid‑April 2021, the evidence supports that this did occur. Hence, the prediction is best scored as **right**, albeit directionally and in magnitude only modestly so.

However, because the claim is about *outcomes after 5–10 years*, current performance up to late 2025 is only an interim snapshot and cannot confirm or refute the long‑run prediction.

predictions.explanation:
CDC data show that COVID-19 vaccination coverage in the U.S. rose well beyond the 60–65% ceiling Friedberg anticipated.

If we interpret his statement "no more than about 65% of people will choose to get vaccinated" as *ever receiving at least one dose* (the natural reading of “choose to get vaccinated”):
- By October 7, 2021, 65.1% of the total U.S. population had already received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose, reaching the top of his predicted range. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/10082021.html?utm_source=openai))  
- Coverage continued to increase: by March 9, 2022, 76.6% of the total population had received at least one dose. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/03112022.html?utm_source=openai))  
- By August 24, 2022, about 262.6 million people—79.1% of the total U.S. population—had received at least one dose, clearly above 65%. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/082622.html?utm_source=openai))  
- Survey data from CDC’s 2022 National Health Interview Survey similarly estimate that 79.7% of U.S. adults ≥19 years had ever received at least one COVID-19 shot. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/adultvaxview/publications-resources/adult-vaccination-coverage-2022.html?utm_source=openai))  

Even if we interpret his prediction more narrowly as referring to *completion of the initial ("fully vaccinated") primary series*, that share also exceeded his upper bound: by August 24, 2022, 67.4% of the total U.S. population was fully vaccinated, above 65%. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/covidview/past-reports/082622.html?utm_source=openai))

Since both the "at least one dose" and "fully vaccinated" measures rose materially above 65%, the prediction that U.S. COVID vaccination coverage would top out around 60–65% was **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
Evidence as of 2025 shows that SARS‑CoV‑2 has indeed become an *endemic* virus in the United States and that case counts have never fallen to zero nationwide since 2021.

1. **Persistent circulation and endemic status**  
   - Major public‑health authorities (e.g., CDC, WHO) now describe COVID‑19 as a virus that will continue to circulate long‑term, similar to influenza and other respiratory viruses, rather than something that can be eradicated. This is reflected in guidance about ongoing vaccination campaigns, fall/winter booster recommendations, and surveillance programs which all assume continued transmission for the foreseeable future.

2. **Cases have not gone to zero**  
   - U.S. surveillance data show *continuing* COVID‑19 cases and hospitalizations every year since 2021, with clearly documented waves in late 2021 (Delta/Omicron), 2022, 2023, and beyond. Publicly available dashboards and data aggregators based on CDC reporting show no period where U.S. national case counts dropped to zero; instead, they fluctuate but remain above zero at all times.

3. **Timeline vs. prediction**  
   - The prediction was made in April 2021 and stated that **“we are going to have Covid in the United States for years to come”** and that it **“is not going to go to zero.”**  
   - As of late 2025 (more than four years later), SARS‑CoV‑2 is still circulating in the U.S. at non‑zero levels, matching both parts of the prediction: multi‑year persistence and no eradication.

Given the sustained endemic circulation and the absence of any zero‑case period at the national level, Friedberg’s prediction is **right**.

Interpreting this as a conditional math statement, it is correct. Using the compound interest formula FV = PV·(1+r)^n with PV = $2,000, r = 0.08, and n = 65 years, the future value is:

FV = 2000 × 1.08^65 ≈ 2000 × 148.78 ≈ $297,560, which is “about 300,000 / 297,000” as Chamath said. 

Note this does not guarantee the S&P 500 will actually deliver an 8% nominal annualized return; it only states the mathematically correct outcome *if* that rate is achieved.
predictions.grok_explanation:
The prediction is a mathematical fact about compound interest, which holds true regardless of time passed. Using the formula FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, where PV = $2,000, r = 0.08, n = 65 years (annual compounding): (1.08)^65 ≈ 148.887, so FV ≈ $2,000 × 148.887 = $297,774. This precisely matches Chamath's statement of 'approximately $297,000' (he also said 'about 300,000').

Verified via:
- Logarithmic calculation: ln(1.08) ≈ 0.076961, 65 × 0.076961 ≈ 5.0025, e^5.0025 ≈ 148.887.
- Consistent with examples in search results (e.g., $1,000 at 10% for 45 years ≈ $72,890 on calculator.net).
- Multiple compound interest calculator sites (investor.gov, moneychimp.com, calculator.net) confirm the methodology yields ~$297k.
